studies.title: Ease Inside The Hardship
studies.meaning: Four favours in the past tense, then a claim repeated word for word, then two instructions. The repetition in the middle is the surah's centre, and the classical grammarians made an argument from the Arabic: the word for hardship carries the definite article both times and the word for ease does not, so the two eases are read as different while the hardship stays one. The last instruction sends the reader from finished work straight into effort again.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, and closely tied to the surah before it, which the classical sources place at the same period and connect to the same situation: a pause in revelation and the taunting that followed. No separate occasion is reported for this one. The favours listed are personal and specific to the one addressed, and the surah is short enough to have been learned in a single hearing.

keyTerms.note: A verb for cutting something open and spreading it flat, used of laying meat open. Applied to a chest it means room made inside a person, and Arabic uses the same image for relief from anxiety.
A verb for the sound a loaded back or a strained joint makes. The burden is described by the noise it caused rather than by its weight, which is a more physical way of saying it was too much.

keyTerms.gloss: so labour, so stand to it
keyTerms.note: An imperative for exerting yourself to the point of fatigue, from a root meaning to set something upright. The instruction is to begin again rather than to rest, and the classical readers connect it to prayer.

The preposition means accompaniment, not sequence. The ease is placed beside the hardship rather than after it, which is the whole difference between this promise and a promise that things will improve.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Carrying was constant work. Water skins, grain sacks and trade goods were moved on backs as much as on animals, and a man who had carried too much for too long walked differently for the rest of his life. Everyone knew the sound of a loaded frame under strain. The surah uses that noise for a burden nobody could see.
studies.didYouKnow: An early saying preserved in the commentaries puts the grammatical point as a slogan: one hardship will never defeat two eases. The reasoning is that the definite article makes the two mentions of hardship a single thing, while the indefinite eases are counted separately. It is one of the best-known pieces of Arabic grammar in the whole tradition.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The promise is about simultaneity rather than sequence, which changes what a person is waiting for. Ease is described as already present inside the difficulty, so the instruction is to look rather than to endure until it passes. The final two lines then refuse rest as the conclusion. Finishing one thing is made the beginning of the next, and the direction of desire is fixed on God rather than on relief.

crossReferences.why: Carries the same argument from remembered favours, and the two surahs are usually read together.
States the same relation in sequence rather than in company, which is the other shape the promise takes.
Uses the same image of an opened chest, asked for rather than granted, at the start of a hard assignment.

studies.applyIt: Take the hardest thing in your week and look for what is easy inside it, not after it. There is usually something: a person who helps, a part you are good at, an hour that is genuinely fine. Name one. The surah puts the ease alongside the difficulty, and the practice is noticing it while the difficulty is still going on.
